item.title: Australian officials ‘working around the clock’ to check welfare of tourists missing in Nepal
item.description:
More than 350 people have been killed, and more than 1,300 people are missing. Prabin RANABHAT / AFP via Getty Images Over 500 foreign tourists are missing after severe floods hit the Nepal-Tibet border region. People from over 30 countries, including Americans, Canadians, and Brits, are among those missing. More than 350 people have died, and more than 1,300 are missing, local authorities said. More than 500 foreign tourists are missing after deadly floods hit the Nepal-Tibet border on Wednesday. The flooding began on the morning of August 26, when a surge of water, mud, and debris entered Nepal from the autonomous Chinese region of Tibet via the Bhote Koshi River, Nepal's Tourism Board said. More than 350 people have died, and more than 1,300 are missing, local authorities said earlier on Thursday, though exact numbers are unclear. The Tourism Board's latest update listed 667 missing…

item.title: UEFA moves to file criminal complaint against Infantino over failed FIFA sell-off
item.description:

item.title: People in Bosnia react to the death of Ratko Mladic, ‘butcher of Bosnia’
item.description:
Bosnian Serb commander responsible for Srebrenica massacre dies in prison while serving life sentence for genocide From the archive: Fourteen years a fugitive: the hunt for the Butcher of Bosnia Ratko Mladić will die in jail. But go to Bosnia: you’ll see that he won Ratko Mladić, the infamous Serbian general who was serving a life sentence for genocide committed during the Bosnian war, has died in prison in The Hague. Mladić had been one of the main architects of the policy of ethnic cleansing during the Bosnian war. He was convicted of genocide for orchestrating the 1995 killing of at least 8,000 Muslims in the UN-designated “safe area” Srebrenica , the worst massacre in Europe since the second world war. item.title: Alleged 9/11 mastermind Khalid Sheikh Mohammed to go on trial in 2028
item.description:
A spokesman for the US military court at Guantanamo Bay said Thursday that Khalid Sheikh Mohammed – the alleged mastermind of the September 11, 2001 attacks on the United States – will go on trial before a US military court in June 2028. Mohammed, also known as "KSM", was considered one of Osama bin Laden's top lieutenants before he was captured in March 2003.

item.title: Bronze age treasure stolen in four-minute Spanish museum heist
item.description:
Enrique Íñiguez (CC-BY-SA) An ancient treasure considered to be a great source of pride for Villena, Spain, has been stolen—part of a slew of robberies across Europe after the Louvre in Paris was broken into last October. A spokesperson said the maneuver was “super-fast and super-professional,” only lasting four minutes. In the early hours of the morning on August 27, thieves arrived in several vehicles, entered through a window, smashed protective glass, and swiped 66 artifacts, which is most of the collection. The exact value of the treasure is incalculable because it dates back to 1000 BCE and includes unique materials—silver, iron, amber, and possibly a rare meteoritic iron that has long stumped scientists. The gold alone is worth €1.7 million ($1.98 million). The alarm in the Villena Museum went off at 5:20 a.m., and another alarm went off at the city’s sports center right before,…

item.title: Nepal flash flood: death toll nears 400 amid warning of fresh danger from rising lake water – latest updates
item.description:
The death toll continues to rise after a catastrophic flood swept through the Nepal-China border, with over 350 people dead and over 1,300 people missing, including at least 60 Americans. Officials in Nepal are worried that the situation could escalate even further with the possibility of a second flood. The director of the Center for Disaster Studies at Tribhuvan University in Nepal, Basanta Raj Adhikari, said “second and third waves” were possible but added, “We don’t know yet.” The flood’s sudden onset is part of what led to the high death toll. Water and debris can travel dozens of miles within hours, leaving the people in its path little to no chance to evacuate before it arrives. That same unpredictability is now complicating the search itself. The potential for more floods threatens rescue crews working the disaster zone. On the ground, Nepal has mobilized nearly 10,000 security…

item.title: Meta reaches $17B settlement. And, nuclear regulator to abandon radiation safety rule
item.description:
Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg chose to settle a landmark lawsuit against his company. Jon Putman/Anadolu via Getty Images Meta has agreed to pay up to US$17 billion over 10 years to settle claims brought by a bipartisan coalition of state attorneys general. The states argued that the company deliberately designed Facebook and Instagram to hook children into using its apps, misled the public about the harm and improperly collected data from children under 13. The settlement , announced by Meta on Aug. 26, 2026, ended a federal trial that had barely begun in Oakland, California. The potential financial exposure in the case was enormous, and Meta’s stock price took a hit. The states argued that penalties could reach hundreds of billions of dollars. item.title: Dolly Parton told us who she was, one song at a time
item.description:
Symbolic urbanism is having a moment, especially this summer in New York City, where the air is far too humid, but the potholes increasingly get filled. | Adam Gray/Bloomberg via Getty Images “If this is democratic socialism,” wrote one New Yorker under a mayoral Facebook post, “maybe it is the change we need.” She was referring neither to Mayor Zohran Mamdani’s heavily scrutinized plan for city-run grocery stores , nor to his pied-à-terre tax on the rich, nor even to his trademark — though thus far, unrealized — vision for fast, free buses and universal childcare . No, she was talking about candy-colored scaffolding .
